summary: Philipp Krenn from Elastic presents on the problems with vector search benchmarking, coining the term "benchmarketing" to describe how vendors produce benchmarks showing their product outperforming all competitors. He identifies several common manipulation tactics. First, vendors cherry-pick scenarios favorable to their system and unfavorable to competitors, or run many scenarios and only publish the favorable one, then generalize it to claim broad superiority. Most benchmarks are read-only with optimized formats, unlike real workloads that involve read-write ratios. A counterintuitive aspect of vector search is that filtering makes HNSW (hierarchical navigable small world) approximate nearest neighbor search slower, not faster, because more candidates must be examined. Vendors often update only their own software while leaving competitor versions stale—sometimes 18 months old—creating unfair comparisons. Implicit biases emerge from knowing how your own system is built, leading to scenario and configuration choices (shard size, memory allocation, instance type) that conveniently favor your system. Cheating includes skipping precision and recall metrics, which are essential in information retrieval but absent in boolean filter searches. Creative statistics can inflate one edge case into a headline claim. Non-reproducible benchmarks lack published configurations. To improve benchmarks, Krenn recommends automation and reproducibility, citing Elastic's nightly benchmarks that catch the "slow boiling frog" problem of incremental performance degradation. Elastic uses a benchmarking tool called Rally, where users create a "track" specifying data and queries, then run and tune it against their own hardware. He firmly states users must build their own benchmarks with their real data sizes, structures, read-write ratios, query patterns, latency requirements, and hardware. In a nuanced closing insight, Krenn advises that even when you find flaws in a benchmark, don't dismiss it entirely—a bad benchmark reveals where the vendor thinks their system's sweet spot lies and what scenario they chose to highlight, which is useful competitive intelligence even from unreliable sources.

sections.title: Introduction to Benchmarketing
sections.summary: Krenn introduces the concept of "benchmarketing," noting that benchmarks exist showing every vendor as both faster and slower than all competitors. He warns against trusting glossy charts and asks the audience about their experience with vector search benchmarks, acknowledging they are notoriously difficult to evaluate.

sections.title: Cherry-Picking Scenarios and Common Manipulation Tactics
sections.summary: Vendors define scenarios that favor their system and disadvantage competitors, or run many scenarios and only publish favorable results while generalizing them. Most benchmarks are read-only with optimized formats, unlike real read-write workloads. Filtering makes HNSW vector search slower rather than faster, a counterintuitive property that can be exploited in benchmark design.

sections.title: Version Skew, Implicit Bias, and Configuration Choices
sections.summary: Vendors update only their own software in benchmarks, sometimes leaving competitor versions 18 months old. Implicit biases arise from knowing your own system's strengths, leading to scenario and configuration choices (shard size, memory, instance type) that conveniently favor your system over competitors, often unintentionally.

sections.title: Cheating, Precision/Recall Omission, and Creative Statistics
sections.summary: Krenn compares benchmark cheating to the Volkswagen emissions scandal. In vector search, cheating often involves omitting precision and recall metrics, making speed comparisons meaningless since poor-quality results can be produced quickly. Creative statistics can inflate one edge case into a broad headline claim. Non-reproducible benchmarks without published configurations further undermine trust.

sections.title: How to Make Benchmarks Better: Nightly Benchmarks and DIY
sections.summary: Krenn recommends automated, reproducible nightly benchmarks to catch the "slow boiling frog" problem of incremental performance degradation. He emphatically states that users must build their own benchmarks with their specific data, queries, latency targets, and hardware, as no vendor benchmark will match their use case. He briefly introduces Elastic's Rally benchmarking tool.

sections.title: Rally Tracks, Learning from Flawed Benchmarks, and Closing
sections.summary: Krenn explains Rally's track mechanism: users define data and queries, run the track, and tune settings or hardware. Rally benchmarks Elastic against itself, not competitors. Users must replicate this approach with other tools for fair comparison. He offers a nuanced final insight: even flawed benchmarks have value because they reveal where vendors believe their system's sweet spot lies and what scenarios they chose to highlight. Dismissing bad benchmarks entirely is easy but less smart than extracting intelligence from them. He closes by reiterating that proper results require building your own benchmarks.

demonstrations: Elastic's nightly benchmarks dashboard shown as example of automated, reproducible performance tracking
limitations: No vendor benchmark will match your specific use case—data size, structure, read-write ratio, query patterns, latency requirements, and hardware all matter
Reproducibility requires publishing all configuration details, which many benchmarks omit
Building your own benchmarks requires significant manual effort with no easy shortcut
Rally only benchmarks Elastic against itself, not against competitors
quantitativeClaims: A competitor benchmark showed 20 data points where 18-19 were similar but one edge case was 10x faster and was generalized into a headline claim
